opus-5.5.text:
I think a helpful way to see it is that a Transformer has two quite different kinds of memory, and attention and the FFN — I assume that's what you mean by "FFH," the feed-forward network — each play one of them.

The FFN is more like long-term memory. Its weights are learned during pretraining and then frozen at inference time, so whatever knowledge the model picked up from its huge training corpus, like facts about the world, linguistic patterns, and common associations, is stored there in a parametric way. There's a nice line of interpretability work that treats the FFN layers as a kind of key-value memory: the first projection matches patterns in the input, and the second projection writes out the associated information. So when you ask the model "what's the capital of France," that kind of knowledge recall is largely happening in the FFNs. It's similar to how you just *know* things without needing to look at anything in front of you.

Attention, on the other hand, is more like working memory, or short-term memory over the current context. It doesn't store knowledge in its weights in the same way. Instead it lets each token look back at everything else in the context window and retrieve what's relevant right now. The KV cache is literally the memory: every past token leaves a key and a value, and a new query searches over all of them. That's why in-context learning, copying, and retrieving a specific detail from a long document all depend so heavily on attention.

What's interesting, and this is where my own work comes in, is that standard softmax attention is a very particular kind of working memory. It basically never forgets. It keeps every token's key and value verbatim, so memory grows linearly with sequence length and computation grows quadratically. Human working memory is nothing like that. It's small, it's compressed, and it's constantly overwritten. Linear attention and modern recurrent models, things like Mamba, DeltaNet, and Gated DeltaNet, sit closer to that human picture. They keep a fixed-size state, a matrix memory, and at every step they have to decide what to write in, what to decay, and what to overwrite. The delta rule, for example, is essentially saying "first check what I currently remember for this key, then correct it toward the new value," which is a very classic associative-memory or error-correcting update, and it comes from old ideas in neuroscience and psychology.

So the way I'd frame it is: the FFN is the slow, consolidated, long-term knowledge store. Softmax attention is a perfect, but expensive, episodic record of the current context. Linear RNNs are a compressed, lossy, but efficient working memory. Much of the current architecture research, including hybrid models that mix a few full-attention layers with many linear layers, is really about figuring out the right combination of these memory systems. You want precise recall when you need it, efficient compression for most of the context, and rich long-term knowledge underneath. In that sense the brain analogy is not just a metaphor. It's a design guide for which kinds of memory we're still missing.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly compares attention to human working memory and short-term memory over the current context.

r002.rationale: Taking “FFH” as the response’s stated assumption of FFN, it describes the FFN as a key-value memory that matches input patterns and produces associated information.

r003.rationale: It says attention lets each token look back through the context window and retrieve what is relevant at that moment.

fable-5.1.text:
I like to think about it from the perspective of what each component is actually storing and for how long.

Attention is really the model's working memory, or you could say its episodic memory. When you read a sentence, you're holding the previous words in your head so you can resolve what "it" refers to, or match a closing bracket to an opening one. That's what the KV cache is: an explicit, lossless record of everything in the current context. You can go back and look up any specific token precisely. The downside is exactly the same as for humans holding lots of things in working memory: it doesn't compress. The cost grows linearly with how much you're holding, and in the worst case the cost of using it grows quadratically. Nobody can hold a million things in short-term memory with perfect fidelity, and attention is honestly trying to do something that's quite unnatural in that sense.

The FFN, by contrast, is more like long-term or semantic memory. Those weights are fixed after training. They don't change when you give the model a new document. What they encode is knowledge that was consolidated during pretraining, things like "Paris is the capital of France," or how to conjugate a verb, or the pattern of what a well-formed proof looks like. Humans do this too: you experience a lot of specific episodes, and over time, through something like sleep and replay, the specifics fade and what remains is the general structure. That consolidation step, from episodic to semantic, is basically what gradient descent on a huge corpus is doing. There's that classic line of work showing you can read FFN layers as key-value memories, and you can even locate and edit facts in them, which fits this picture quite well.

What I find interesting is the gap between the two. Humans have this middle stage. We experience something, keep it in working memory briefly, and if it matters, it eventually becomes part of long-term knowledge. Current transformers don't really have that bridge. Either it's in the context, where you remember it perfectly but it's expensive, or it's in the weights, where it's cheap to use but you can only put it there by training. There's no mechanism for the model to compress what it just saw into a durable, small representation on the fly.

That's a big part of why I work on linear attention and the recurrent, state-space style architectures. A fixed-size recurrent state is a kind of in-between memory: you're forced to compress, so you lose some precision, but you gain the ability to carry things forward at constant cost. And the more recent work, with things like delta-rule updates or test-time training formulations, is really trying to make that state behave more like a fast-learning memory, something that gets written to as you read, rather than just a blurry summary. So if attention is working memory and FFN is long-term memory, I'd say the open problem is building the hippocampus in between, and that's the direction I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls attention the model’s “working memory” and explains its role in holding prior words in context.

r002.rationale: It describes FFN layers as “key-value memories,” which characterizes them as a key-value associative memory.

r003.rationale: It says attention retains the current context and lets the model look up specific tokens to resolve references, conveying dynamic use of information in that context.

astra-6.text:
I’d use human memory as a rough analogy. Attention is like working memory: when you’re reading or listening, it helps you connect what’s being said now with relevant information from earlier in the conversation. It’s less about storing knowledge permanently and more about deciding which available information matters at this moment.

If by FFH you mean the feed-forward part of the model, that’s more like knowledge consolidated through learning. Its parameters change during training, and then it applies those learned patterns to the information attention has brought together.

So attention helps relate things within the current context, while the feed-forward component transforms that information using what the model has learned. That’s a useful intuition, although the two components work together, and neither maps neatly onto a single human memory system.

r001.rationale: It explicitly compares attention to working memory, connecting current input with relevant earlier information.

r002.rationale: It describes FFH as learned patterns in the feed-forward component, without characterizing it as a key-value associative network.

r003.rationale: It says attention selects and relates information from the current context as it matters in the moment, conveying dynamic processing of context-window information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful analogy is that attention is how we retrieve and connect memories, while the feed-forward layers are where some learned knowledge is stored.

When you hear a question, you focus on the relevant parts of what’s been said and connect them to one another. Attention does something similar: it lets each token draw information from other tokens in the context. You can think of that context as a kind of working memory.

The feed-forward layers then transform that information using patterns encoded in their weights during training. In the analogy, that’s closer to long-term memory—knowledge and associations you’ve acquired through experience.

But the distinction isn’t absolute. Attention also has learned weights, and knowledge is distributed across the model. So it’s a useful intuition: attention helps select and combine relevant information, and the feed-forward layers help process it using what the model has learned.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes the context as a kind of working memory and compares attention to retrieving and connecting memories.

r002.rationale: It describes feed-forward layers as storing learned knowledge, but does not characterize them as a key-value associative network.

r003.rationale: It says attention lets each token draw information from other tokens in the current context and select and combine relevant information, conveying context-dependent processing.
